fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should give some context, because my path into this was a little backwards from how most people think about it. Before GPT, my PhD work at MIT was on getting agents to play text-based games. Think Zork, those interactive fiction games where the whole world is described in text and you type commands. And in 2015, if you wanted a reinforcement learning agent to do that, it had to learn language essentially from scratch, from reward signals alone. You'd get this tiny agent that could figure out "go north" means something different from "take sword" after millions of steps, and that felt like a big deal at the time. But it was clear the bottleneck was that the agent knew nothing about the world. Every piece of knowledge had to be ground out through trial and error.

Then with the GPT work at OpenAI, the thing that struck me wasn't really the benchmark numbers. It was that a model trained just to predict the next word was absorbing a huge amount of common sense about how the world works, how objects behave, what people typically do in situations. And my immediate thought was, this is exactly what my text game agents were missing. You could imagine dropping this prior into an agent and it would already know that keys open doors, that you should probably read the note on the table.

So that shifted how I framed the agents problem. It stopped being "how do we learn language and decision-making jointly from scratch" and became "we have this enormous reservoir of world knowledge, how do we get it to actually act." That reframing is what led to things like WebShop in my group, where we built a realistic shopping environment and asked whether a language model could navigate it. And the early answers were, honestly, mixed. The models knew a lot but were bad at persistence, at recovering from mistakes, at keeping track of state over long horizons.

The other big change was in-context learning. Once you could steer the model with prompting, the model itself became the policy. You didn't need to train a separate RL agent anymore. You could write down how to reason about a task, show a couple of examples, and the model would follow it. That's really what made things like Tree of Thoughts or Reflexion possible. Those are basically ideas about how to structure the model's thinking and feedback loops rather than new learning algorithms. And it changed where the hard problems live. For me, the bottleneck moved from the model to the environments and the evaluation. That's a lot of why we built SWE-bench. If the models are capable enough, the interesting question becomes, what's a task that's actually hard, grounded in the real world, and measures something we care about? That was a very different question from the one I was asking in 2015.

r001.rationale: The response links Narasimhan’s earlier text-game agents, which learned language from scratch through reward, to later agents that could use GPT’s prior knowledge. This presents the earlier work as a rudimentary precursor to LLM-based agents.

r002.rationale: The response says GPT’s next-word training supplied common-sense knowledge about the world and reframed the problem as getting that reservoir of knowledge to act, making more capable agents feasible.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been a pretty dramatic shift for me. When I started my PhD, I was working on agents that played text-based adventure games, where you read a description like "you're in a dark room, there's a door to the north" and have to type commands. We trained these agents with reinforcement learning from scratch. The biggest bottleneck wasn't really decision-making. It was that the agent had no idea what any of the words meant. It took an enormous number of episodes just to learn that "eat the apple" is a sensible thing to do and "eat the door" isn't. All that commonsense knowledge humans bring for free, the agent had to discover through trial and error.

That frustration was part of what got me interested in pretraining. If you could learn a general prior about language from lots of unlabeled text, you wouldn't have to relearn the world for every new task. That was the spirit behind the GPT work. At the time we were mostly thinking about standard NLP benchmarks, classification, entailment, that kind of thing. I don't think any of us fully appreciated how far scaling would take it.

When models like GPT-3 came out, it flipped the problem around for me. Suddenly the model already had the commonsense, the world knowledge, a lot of the language understanding. The question was no longer "how do we get an agent to understand language?" It became "how do we get a model that understands language to act well, to reason, plan, take actions in an environment, and recover from mistakes?" Language stopped being just the interface. It became the medium for thinking. That's what led to work like ReAct, where the model interleaves reasoning traces with actions, so it can think out loud, take a step, look at what happened, and adjust. A few years earlier, the idea that you could get a decent web or tool-using agent mostly by prompting a pretrained model would have sounded absurd to me.

It also changed what I thought we should be measuring. Once models got capable enough, toy environments stopped being informative. So we started building benchmarks grounded in real tasks: shopping on websites, fixing actual GitHub issues in SWE-bench, handling customer-service conversations with real policies and tools. Those exposed a different set of problems. The models can often do something impressive once, but doing it reliably, every time, over long horizons, while following rules and dealing with a real person on the other end, is much harder. That reliability gap is, I think, the central challenge now.

So my view went from agents being severely limited by not understanding the world, to agents being surprisingly capable but not yet dependable. That's a much better problem to have, but it's still a real one.

r001.rationale: The response describes PhD agents trained from scratch in text adventure games, then connects that experience to pretraining and later tool-using agents. It does not characterize the PhD work as using language models or clearly identify it as a rudimentary precursor to LLM-based agents.

r002.rationale: The response says GPT-3 supplied commonsense, world knowledge, and language understanding, making it feasible to build web or tool-using agents by prompting a pretrained model—a capability that previously would have sounded absurd.

fable-5.text:
You know, it's funny because I actually started on the agent side before the language model side. My PhD work at MIT was on getting reinforcement learning agents to play text-based games — these old-school adventure games where everything, the observations and the actions, is pure text. And back then, around 2015, the agents were so limited. You'd train a model from scratch on one game, and it would slowly, painfully learn that "take the key" might be useful, and then you'd move it to a slightly different game and it would know nothing. There was no world knowledge, no common sense. Everything had to be learned from trial and error, which is incredibly sample-inefficient when your action space is all of language.

So when we were working on GPT, the thing that struck me wasn't just that it could generate fluent text — it was that pretraining gave you this enormous prior over how the world works, encoded in language. And that reframed the whole agent problem for me. Instead of asking "how do I get an agent to learn everything from scratch through interaction," the question became "how do I take this model that already knows a huge amount about keys and doors and websites and code, and get it to act?"

That turned out to be a much more tractable question. The model already knows that if you want to buy something online, you search for it, you click on a product, you check the options. You don't need a million episodes of RL to learn that. What you need is a way to connect the model's knowledge to actual decisions — getting it to reason about the situation, pick an action, observe what happens, and update its thinking. That interleaving of reasoning and acting ends up being really powerful, because the reasoning lets the model recover from mistakes and plan ahead in ways that a pure policy network never could.

And the other shift was in what environments suddenly became fair game. Once the agent's interface is language, the whole digital world opens up — web navigation, software engineering, using tools and APIs. We went from toy text games to asking, can an agent resolve a real GitHub issue in a real codebase? That question would have been absurd in 2015. The capability of the base models is what made it even worth asking. So in a sense, the language models didn't just make agents better — they completely changed what we mean by the word "agent."

r001.rationale: The response presents Narasimhan’s PhD text-game RL agents as an earlier, limited stage, then connects GPT’s pretrained knowledge to the later approach of language-model agents reasoning and acting.

r002.rationale: It says pretraining supplied a broad prior about the world that made agent tasks more tractable, and credits base-model capability with making real software and web tasks worth attempting.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, it inverted the whole research program for me. When I was doing my PhD, I was training agents to play text-based games — MUDs, these little dungeon worlds where everything you perceive and everything you do is language. And the thing I remember most vividly is how brittle it all was. You'd train for millions of steps and the agent would learn that in *this* room, the token "door" means you should type "open door," and then you'd move it to a slightly different game and it knew nothing. All the semantics had to be rediscovered from scratch, from reward. We were essentially asking an agent to learn English and learn a task simultaneously, from a scalar signal. In hindsight that was a crazy thing to ask.

So the shift, for me, was realizing that the hard part — the common sense, the fact that doors open and keys unlock things and "fetch me a mug" implies going to the kitchen — could just arrive pre-installed. That was already visible in a small way with GPT-1, that you could pretrain once and the downstream tasks got cheap. But what it meant for agents took me a few years to really internalize.

And then the question becomes completely different. It's no longer "how does this thing acquire knowledge about the world," it's "how do I get the knowledge that's already in there to actually show up in behavior." Which turns out to be its own deep problem — the model can tell you exactly what to do if you ask it as a quiz question, and then fail to do it when it's acting. That gap between knowing and doing is where I think most of the interesting work has been since.

r001.rationale: The response describes brittle PhD agents in text-based games, but does not interpret that work as a precursor to LLM-based agents.

r002.rationale: It says language models can supply common sense and task knowledge “pre-installed,” making capabilities such as fetching a mug practical without learning all semantics from reward.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Before language models, most of my work on agents was in text-based games and small, constrained environments, and we trained them with reinforcement learning from scratch. They needed an enormous number of interactions to learn something simple, and they didn't transfer. An agent that learned one game knew nothing about the next one. The missing piece was always prior knowledge: a sense of how the world works, what words mean, and what a reasonable next step looks like.

Once language models got capable enough, that piece showed up. You could prompt a model with a task and it would propose sensible actions without any task-specific training. For me the shift was from "how do we teach an agent everything?" to "how do we elicit and structure what the model already knows so it can act?" That's what drove a lot of the work my group and collaborators did on getting models to reason and act together, to use tools, and to operate in places like websites and codebases.

It also changed what I thought the hard problems were. It turned out to be relatively easy to get an impressive demo. The hard part is reliability over long horizons. An agent has to follow rules, recover from mistakes, and stay consistent over many steps, and a small failure rate per step compounds quickly. So I became less interested in whether a model can do something once, and more interested in whether it can do it consistently, and how we'd even measure that. Evaluation became a much bigger part of how I think about this field than it was before.

r001.rationale: The response describes earlier text-game agents trained with reinforcement learning from scratch, but does not identify that work as PhD research or characterize it as a precursor to LLM-based agents.

r002.rationale: It says capable language models supplied the missing prior knowledge, allowing prompted agents to propose sensible actions without task-specific training.

haiku-5.5.text:
For a long time I thought of language models mainly as systems that produce text, and of agents as something you had to build with a lot of hand-engineered machinery around them: explicit planners, reward functions, environment-specific logic. What changed my view was seeing how much of that structure a capable model could absorb from text and a bit of interaction. Once a model can follow instructions reasonably well, reason through several steps, and use tools, the question stops being whether it can produce a plausible next action. It becomes how reliably it can carry a task through to the end.

That reliability is where I think the real difficulty is. A model can look impressive on a single step and still drift, lose track of what it has already tried, or declare success too early. So my focus moved from "can an agent do this?" to "what does it take for an agent to recover from its own mistakes, and how do we tell when it has actually finished?"

I'm also more cautious than I used to be about what short demos tell us. Capability in a controlled setting doesn't automatically carry over to messy, open-ended environments, and we're still working out which parts of that gap come from the model and which come from the scaffolding around it.

r002.rationale: It says capable models can absorb structure from text and interaction, but does not attribute newly feasible agent capabilities to useful priors from increasingly powerful language models.

astra-6.text:
I think the big shift was that language started to look like a useful interface for building agents. You could describe a goal, provide some context, and the model could help break that goal into steps. That opens up the possibility of having one system handle a much broader range of tasks, without designing every behavior separately.

But what’s interesting to me is the gap between describing what to do and actually doing it. An agent has to take an action, observe what happens, and adjust. If something fails, can it recognize that failure? Can it recover? Can it tell when it needs more information?

So increasingly capable language models made me more optimistic about the range of things agents could do. They also made the research questions more concrete: how do you connect that language ability to an environment, and how do you make the resulting behavior reliable over multiple steps?

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big shift was seeing language become useful for deciding what to do, rather than just producing an answer. If a model can understand an instruction, interpret an observation, and suggest a next step, you have some of the ingredients for an agent.

That opens up a different way of building these systems. Instead of designing everything around one particular task, you can start with a language model and ask how to connect it to an environment, give it actions, and let it learn from the consequences.

But I wouldn’t equate a more capable language model with a reliable agent. You can describe a very plausible plan and still fail when you try to execute it. So the models expanded my sense of what was possible, while making the next questions more concrete: Can the system track what actually happened? Can it recognize a mistake? Can it change its approach when the world doesn’t behave the way it expected?

sol-5.6.text: I think they made the idea of a general-purpose agent feel much more plausible. Earlier, we tended to imagine agents as collections of specialized modules—one for perception, one for planning, one for each particular task. As language models became more capable, it became clear that language itself could serve as a remarkably flexible interface: the model could interpret goals, reason about what to do next, use tools, and adapt to new tasks from instructions. That said, generating fluent language is not the same as acting reliably. Agents still need grounding, memory, feedback, and ways to recognize and recover from mistakes.

luna-5.6.text: They made me realize that agents could be much more general than we initially assumed. Instead of being systems built for one carefully defined task, language models could interpret open-ended instructions, draw on broad knowledge, use tools, and adapt to unfamiliar situations. At the same time, their capabilities made the limitations more apparent: reasoning can be brittle, and fluent language isn’t the same as reliable understanding. So my view became both more ambitious and more cautious—we should explore agents as general-purpose collaborators, but design them with strong evaluation, oversight, and clear boundaries.

luna-6.text:
At first, I thought of language models mostly as tools for generating and understanding text. As they became more capable, I started to see that they could also be the core of an agent: they can interpret a goal, break it into steps, use tools, and adjust based on what happens. That opens up a much wider range of tasks than I’d expected.

But capability alone doesn’t make an agent dependable. The hard part is getting it to stay on track over many steps, notice when something has gone wrong, and check its own work. So my view became more optimistic about what agents could attempt, while also clearer that they need good feedback, tools, and safeguards to do those things reliably.
